description:
Team RedVector is tackling the Martian Map challenge in Space Apps 2026! We're building a multi-layered mapping tool for Mars exploration using NASA data.

We have strong Software & Web Dev skills and are looking for teammates with experience in GIS/Data Viz, UI/UX Design, Planetary Science, or Technical Writing. Join us!
summary: MarsWalk is a browser-based planner and simulator for one Marswalk (EVA) at a real site: the boxwork ridges on Mount Sharp in Gale Crater, which Curiosity explored in 2025. On a 10 m terrain map built from a HiRISE-derived elevation model, an astronaut picks a base and a destination. A* search, running in a Web Worker, plans a Shortest, Balanced or Safest route. It reports distance, climb, walking time and oxygen for the walk out and back, gives a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict, and draws a point-of-no-return map of where the astronaut can still get home on the oxygen left. A timed simulation, in 3D or in an educational 2D view, then injects emergencies (dust storm, suit leak, rockfall, injury, solar particle event) and replans from the astronaut's current position. The map layers combine data from four NASA missions: MGS MOLA, MRO CTX and HiRISE, Mars Odyssey THEMIS, and Curiosity's positions, Navcam images and measured REMS weather and RAD radiation. This answers the challenge's call for a hyperlocal map that turns terrain into survival decisions. It also labels which numbers are measured and which are model assumptions.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
MarsWalk helps an astronaut plan, rehearse and debrief a single Marswalk. It works at three scales: a whole-Mars overview, a Gale Crater overview (1.85 km cells, from MGS MOLA) and a hyperlocal map of the boxwork area (10 m cells over a 4 km square, from the USGS MSL Gale Merged DEM, which is derived from MRO HiRISE stereo images).

HOW IT WORKS

  1. Data preparation (Python, NumPy): scripts read NASA archive files, crop each region, compute slope with east-west spacing corrected for latitude, and write small, deterministic web assets. The 1 m elevation model is read with HTTP range requests, so only the part we need is downloaded.
  2. Route planning: A* search on an 8-neighbour grid, running in a Web Worker. Each step costs its ground distance plus slope and elevation-change penalties. Ground steeper than 25° counts as impassable; that is Curiosity's maximum recorded pitch, a rover figure. Walking speed follows Tobler's hiking function. Oxygen use comes from an Apollo EVA average metabolic rate (234 kcal/h) at 4.8 kcal per litre of O2.
  3. Point of no return: the way back is not the way out reversed, because uphill and downhill cost differently. So a separate search runs backwards from the base. It gives the oxygen needed to get home from every cell, and marks where on the route the astronaut must turn back.
  4. Simulation: the astronaut walks the route in compressed time, with a suit display showing oxygen left, oxygen needed to get home, and the margin. An emergency opens a timed decision card. The options are recomputed from the astronaut's current position, and one is recommended. There are two roles, EVA astronaut and Mission Control. Runs are seeded so they can be repeated. Each run ends with a "black box" debrief: a chart of the oxygen margin and a table of every decision.
  5. Educational view: every number is explained step by step (grade, then walking speed, then time, then oxygen). Shortest, Balanced and Safest routes are compared side by side. Every fact is tagged as computed, model assumption or verified.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

  • Turns raw terrain into the questions an EVA crew actually asks: Can I get there? Can I get back? How much science time do I have? What happens if something goes wrong?
  • Trains judgement: one engine serves both the astronaut and Mission Control, and the debrief shows each call that differed from the suit computer's recommendation.
  • Teaches: students and the public see how orbital and rover data become a walking plan, and which parts are measured and which are assumed.
  • Open to anyone: it is fully static and free to host (GitHub Pages), runs on laptops and on phones in landscape, and needs no account and no server.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE
Python with NumPy, Pillow and imagecodecs (data preparation). TypeScript, Vite and MapLibre GL JS (2D maps). Three.js (3D walk and airlock). Web Workers (route planning). Sound synthesised in the browser and the browser's built-in speech voices. Vitest (84 unit tests, including A* checked against Dijkstra and the return search checked against a brute-force reference). GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages (test, build and deploy).

WHAT IS CREATIVE

  • The start screen is a 3D airlock. It depressurises from Earth pressure to the 743 Pa that Curiosity's REMS measured, then opens onto the real terrain, turned toward the most open view computed from the elevation skyline.
  • The data package "uplinked from Earth" is the real set of files the app loads.
  • A first-person 3D walk on the 10 m terrain mesh at true vertical scale, draped with the CTX photo, with synthesised wind, breathing and radio.
  • A point-of-no-return map and a turn-back marker, instead of a plain route line.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  • Data honesty: walking, energy and oxygen rates are model assumptions, not suit specifications, and the oxygen reserves are demo values. Conditions are historical measurements at Curiosity's position, not forecasts: sol 4598, 743 Pa, −82.9 to −17.3 °C, and 167.9 µGy/day, which is a detector dose, not a body dose.
  • Accuracy: our first cut of the 1 m elevation model sat about 840 m from its true position. We found the shift by correlating the terrain with the CTX photo and corrected it. The model now matches Curiosity's own recorded elevations to within 9 m and 1.3 m at the two waypoints.
  • Resolution limits: a 10 m cell can miss features narrower than itself. Both science stops sit on narrow ridge crests, so their routes end at the nearest walkable cell (14 m and 20 m away), and the app says so.
  • Reliability: there is no server and no live map-tile requests, and the 2D view is a fallback when 3D runs slowly.

USE OF AI
Claude Code (Anthropic) wrote most of the code, tests and documentation drafts, under the team's direction. ChatGPT suggested candidate data sources and drafted some task instructions. GitHub Copilot ran one testing and documentation audit. Every dataset, URL and number was checked against its source before use. Details are in the README section "AI usage disclosure" and in log.txt.

MRO CTX Gale mosaic, Gale_CTX_BlockAdj_dd (NASA Mars Trek WMTS)
Mars Odyssey THEMIS qualitative thermal inertia, Gale (ASU THEMIS archive)
Curiosity (MSL) PLACES rover localizations (PDS Imaging Node)
Curiosity REMS calibrated weather data, sols 4489–4612 (PDS Atmospheres Node)
Curiosity RAD radiation RDR, sols 4489–4612 (PDS PPI Node)
